To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the presence of immunoblasts in the blood of patients with active rheumatic disease is related to the disease activity and may provide an early indication of a relapse; (2) immunoblasts are also seen in idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura, but not in aplastic anaemia; (3) immunoblast formation is not specific to the autoimmune diseases and may also be seen following infection and immunization.
the lymphoid cell populations from the blood of patients with autoimmune diseases are different from those of patients with other diseases.

the lymphoid cells in patients with autoimmune disorders show reactive changes that are identical with those in patients with infections, following immunization, and in normal individuals, and that these changes are not seen in patients with aplastic anemia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of lymphoid cells to study the immune system in health and disease.
the study of the lymphoid cells in the peripheral blood of patients with autoimmune disorders, and with haematological disorders of unknown aetiology.
the study of the immune response in man and the relationship of this to the development of disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lymphoid cell population in the peripheral blood is not normal in autoimmune disease, and the changes seen are probably related to the activity and severity of the disorder.

the presence of reactive lymphocytes in the peripheral blood of patients with active autoimmune disorders and infections, and after immunization, provides supporting evidence that these conditions have an autoimmune basis.

reactive lymphoid cells in autoimmune disease and haematological conditions are not specific for any particular disease, but may be of value in indicating the activity of the autoimmune disease, and also in providing supportive evidence for the autoimmune basis of certain haematological conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
reactive lymphoid cell populations are seen in a number of autoimmune disorders, and that these changes are not specific to any particular disease.
the presence of reactive lymphoid cells ('immunoblasts') indicates that an autoimmune disease is active, whereas their absence does not exclude an autoimmune aetiology for that disease.
reactive lymphoid cells ('immunoblasts') can be seen in a wide range of disorders but are not a reliable marker of autoimmunity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown for the first time that a specific subset of T cells, which we have called 'T helper 1 cells', are responsible for the autoimmune disease in the NZB mouse.
the lymphoid cell population of the blood is an extremely sensitive indicator of the presence of autoimmunity.
we need to be more careful about the use of the term "autoimmunity" when describing diseases of unknown origin.
